title: Fiqh close
hookLine: many schools, many scholars, one book, one sunnah

cards: A shelf, to start. On it sits one Qur'an and a few volumes of hadith.

Beside it stands a whole wall: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali books, Ja'fari, Zaydi and Ibadi books, commentaries on commentaries, rulings on wedding gifts, on contracts, on donkeys carrying too much, on hospital beds.
For weeks this path has walked along that wall. Today the walk ends, with one last question: how does one small shelf turn into a wall, and still face the same way?

teach.b: Start with the word. Fiqh means understanding.
In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that when Allah wants good for someone, He gives that person understanding in the religion, and the verb comes from the same root as fiqh.
So the whole wall is people trying to understand.
Next, the roads. The jurists started from the same place: the Qur'an first, the sunnah second. Then they reasoned out.

Some leaned on the agreement of scholars, some on analogy, some on reason itself, as Ja'fari jurists do, some on the common good or the custom of a place. Different tools, different roads. Then, the difference.
The Qur'an gives a direction for disputes: "if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger." The schools all claim that same reference point.
And Bukhari records a hadith that explains their patience with each other: a judge who strives and gets it right has two rewards, and one who strives and gets it wrong still has one.
Effort in good faith is honored even when it misses. Last, the direction. Stand at the back of a mosque at prayer time.
One person folds the hands high, another lets them hang. One says amin aloud, another under the breath.
Every row still faces the same point.

how: Muslims follow the rulings of a school of law or a trusted scholar, and when a jurist's name is mentioned a Muslim may add a phrase asking Allah's mercy for them.

o: the final ruling that settles every school's debates
the end of the law block: many schools, one source
a list of rulings every school has agreed to drop

games.q: the close of fiqh — tap the pairs.
p: a judge who strives and errs

s: a scholar who reasons carefully and gets it wrong earns nothing
a hadith in Bukhari says he still has one reward; the one who gets it right has two.
the schools all start from the Qur'an and the sunnah
they differ in the tools they use next, not in that starting point.
different hands in prayer means a different direction
people fold or lower their hands differently, and every row still faces the same point.

games.q: two jurists, both careful and sincere, reach different answers on the same question. what does the hadith say about them?
o: only the one who is right is rewarded.
the one who is right has two rewards, and the one who errs has one.
neither is rewarded until they agree.
games.why: the hadith in Bukhari honors the effort itself: two rewards for getting it right, one for striving and missing.

practice: Bring one name to mind, someone who did the slow work of understanding: Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ja'far al-Sadiq, or someone closer, a teacher, an imam, a grandmother who knew how to pray and showed you.
If you pray, you may know the custom of asking Allah's mercy for a scholar when the name comes up; if you don't, simply say thank you, in your own head.

wordCard.voice: Fiqh close. The end of the block on fiqh, the understanding of the law: one book, one sunnah, many schools working from them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: understanding; the name for the study of Islamic law.

carryVoice: Your line: many roads, one direction. Tomorrow a new block starts: belief. See you there.
